- Out of scope: brings in a topic the passage never discusses, such as the colors of freshwater fish or how predators see color.
- Reversed: says the opposite of what the passage says, or swaps cause and effect.
- True but irrelevant: matches something in the passage but does not answer the question asked.
- Half right: begins correctly and then adds a claim the passage does not support. Read every choice to its last word.
! A choice that repeats the passage's exact words is not automatically right. The GRE often reuses passage vocabulary in wrong answers, and paraphrases the correct one.
## Timing

Plan about 1.5 to 2 minutes per question including reading, so roughly 3 to 4 minutes for a short passage and its two questions. Spend about a minute on the first read and map, then answer. If a question is taking much longer than 90 seconds on its own, eliminate what you can, choose, mark it, and return to it later if time allows.
## Quick checklist
- Did I build a map: topic, purpose, the role of each sentence?
- For each question, did I find the supporting line before choosing?
- For select-all, did I judge each choice separately?
- Did I reject choices that are too extreme, out of scope, reversed, irrelevant or only half right?

title: Sentence Equivalence
lines: ## What you see on screen

A sentence equivalence item shows one sentence with one blank and six answer choices, each with a small square box. The instructions ask you to select exactly two choices that both complete the sentence and produce two sentences that are alike in meaning.

You earn credit only if both choices are correct. One right and one wrong scores zero. So the task is not "find two synonyms"; it is "find the two words that fit this sentence and say the same thing in it".
## How the six choices are built
In a typical item, the six choices contain:
- the correct pair: two words that fit the clue and mean nearly the same thing in context;
- a trap pair: two words that are synonyms of each other but do not fit the sentence;
- one or two loners: a word that fits the sentence reasonably well but has no partner among the choices, plus filler words that fit nothing.
Understanding this structure is a strategy in itself. A pair of synonyms is a candidate, not an answer. A word that fits but has no partner cannot be correct, because you need two.
## The method step by step
- Step 1: Read the sentence and ignore the choices, exactly as in text completion.
- Step 2: Find the clue and the signal word (contrast, continuation, cause and effect), and decide the charge and degree of the blank.
- Step 3: Predict your own word for the blank.
- Step 4: Scan all six choices and mark every word that matches your prediction. Usually you will find exactly two.
- Step 5: Check the pair. Plug in each word separately and read the sentence twice. Do both versions make sense, and do they mean the same thing?
- Step 6: If you found only one match, look for its closest partner among the remaining words; if you found three, test which two are closest to each other and to the sentence.
## Worked example: a clean pair
> Though the new manager had a reputation for being ____, she proved surprisingly willing to change course when her team presented fresh data.
> Choices: obstinate, flexible, intransigent, perceptive, gregarious, tactful.
> Signal: "Though" (contrast). Clue: "surprisingly willing to change course". So the reputation was the opposite of willing to change. Prediction: stubborn.

> "Obstinate" and "intransigent" (refusing to compromise) both match and create sentences with the same meaning. "Flexible" is the opposite trap. "Perceptive", "gregarious" (sociable) and "tactful" are qualities a manager might have, but none is opposed to changing course.
## Worked example: the synonym trap pair
> The documentary's narration was so ____ that viewers who knew nothing about geology could follow every step of the argument.
> Choices: lucid, abstruse, pellucid, esoteric, lengthy, animated.
> Clue: viewers with no background could follow every step. Prediction: clear.
> "Lucid" and "pellucid" (both meaning very clear and easy to understand) form the correct pair.
> "Abstruse" and "esoteric" are a genuine synonym pair, both meaning hard to understand or known only to specialists. They are the trap: two words that agree with each other but contradict the clue.
> "Animated" (lively) is a loner: a lively narration might help viewers, but it says nothing about clarity, and no other choice means lively.
## Worked example: a loner that fits
> The committee's response to the proposal was ____: members praised its goals but raised so many objections that no vote was taken.
> Choices: ambivalent, enthusiastic, equivocal, hostile, indifferent, delayed.
> Clue: praise mixed with many objections. Prediction: mixed, undecided.
> "Ambivalent" (having mixed feelings) and "equivocal" (uncertain, not committing either way) form the pair.

> "Delayed" is the loner that fits the facts, because no vote was taken, so the response was in a sense delayed. But it does not describe the mixed praise and objections, and no other choice means delayed. "Enthusiastic" and "hostile" each capture only half of the clue.
## When words fit but change the meaning
The test requires sentences alike in meaning, so two words that both fit can still fail if they push the sentence in different directions.
> The sudden rise in sales left analysts ____.

> "Baffled" and "delighted" can both complete this sentence grammatically, yet one says the analysts were confused and the other says they were pleased. They are not a pair. "Baffled" and "perplexed" would be.
Pay special attention to degree. "Displeased" and "livid" are both negative, but one is mild and one is extreme, so they do not produce equivalent sentences.
## When you do not know some of the words
Sentence equivalence is the most vocabulary-heavy question type, so you will often meet a word you are unsure of. Work in this order:
- Eliminate the words you know do not fit.
- Look for a pair among the words you know.
- If you know only one word that fits, its partner is likely an unknown word, not a known word that fails the sentence.
- If two unknown words remain and you need one of them, use roots and the company each word keeps, then guess. There is no penalty for a wrong answer.
! Do not choose a pair just because the two words look alike or share a root. "Disinterested" (impartial) and "uninterested" (bored) look similar but mean different things.
## Traps the GRE sets
! The synonym-pair trap: two words that clearly mean the same thing but do not fit the clue. Always test fit before you test similarity.
! The loner trap: a word that fits the sentence well but has no partner. If you cannot find its match, drop it.
! The opposite trap: a word that means the reverse of the answer, aimed at readers who missed a contrast signal.
! The near-miss pair: two words in the same general area but of different degree or different shade (frugal and stingy, for example: one is praise, the other is criticism).
! The secondary-meaning trap: a common word used in a rarer sense, such as "arrest" meaning stop or "sanction" meaning approve (or, in other contexts, penalize).
## Timing

Aim for about one minute per item; with a clear prediction, many take 40 seconds. Because a wrong pair scores zero, it is worth taking a few extra seconds for Step 5, the reread of each word in the sentence. If you are stuck between two possible pairs, choose the pair whose words are closest to each other in meaning and degree, mark the item, and move on.
## Quick checklist
- Did I predict a word before looking at the six choices?
- Do both of my words fit the clue in the sentence?
- Do the two completed sentences mean the same thing, at the same strength?
- Did I reject the synonym pair that does not fit and the loner with no partner?

title: Statistics
lines: GRE statistics is about describing a list of numbers: where its centre is, how spread out it is, and where one value sits relative to the rest. You will rarely compute a standard deviation, but you must understand what changes it.
## Mean
- Mean = sum ÷ number of values, so sum = mean × number of values. Work with sums: they turn average questions into simple arithmetic.
- Adding a value above the mean raises the mean; below it, lowers it; equal to it, leaves it unchanged.
> Sofia's mean on four tests is 82. What must she score on the fifth for a mean of 85?
> Sum needed = 5 × 85 = 425. Sum so far = 4 × 82 = 328.
> Fifth score = 425 − 328 = 97.
## Median, mode and range
- Median: the middle value after sorting. With an even count, the mean of the two middle values.
- Mode: the most frequent value (a list can have several modes or none).
- Range: largest minus smallest.
> For 7, 3, 9, 3, 12, 5 find the mean, median, mode and range.
! Always sort before finding a median. The middle of the unsorted list (9 and 3 here) means nothing.
! An extreme value pulls the mean but barely moves the median. In a list with one very large value, the mean is above the median.
## Standard deviation as a concept
- Standard deviation (SD) measures how far values typically are from the mean. All values equal gives SD 0.
- Adding the same number to every value shifts the mean but leaves the SD unchanged. Multiplying every value by k multiplies the SD by |k|.
- Values bunched near the mean give a small SD; values far out on both sides give a large one, even with the same mean and range.
> Which set has the larger SD: {8, 10, 12} or {2, 10, 18}?
> Both have mean 10, but the second set's values are 8 away from the mean instead of 2. Its SD is larger (four times as large).
> For the curious: the eight values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 have mean 5. The squared distances add to 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 32; 32/8 = 4, and √4 = 2, so the SD is 2.
! In QC, compare spreads by eye: you almost never need the formula. Adding a value equal to the mean shrinks the SD slightly; adding a value far from the mean increases it.
## Weighted averages
- Weighted mean = (sum of each group mean × group size) ÷ total size.
- The combined mean lies between the group means, closer to the larger group.
> Class A has 20 students with a mean of 70; class B has 30 with a mean of 80. Find the combined mean.
> Not 75: class B is larger, so the result leans toward 80.
## Quartiles, percentiles and box plots
- Quartiles split sorted data into four groups of equal count. Q2 is the median; Q1 is the median of the lower half; Q3 the median of the upper half.
- Interquartile range (IQR) = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle half of the data.
- The pth percentile is a value with about p% of the data at or below it. Q1 is the 25th percentile and Q3 the 75th.
- A box plot shows five numbers: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box holds the middle 50%; each whisker holds 25%.
> Twelve values: median = (10 + 12)/2 = 11.
> IQR = 16.5 − 6 = 10.5. A box plot would run from 2 to 23 with the box from 6 to 16.5 and a line at 11.
! A long whisker or a wide part of the box does not hold more values; every quarter holds the same count. Width shows spread, not frequency.
! Percentile is not percent correct. A score at the 90th percentile beat about 90% of test takers; it says nothing about how many questions were right.
## The normal distribution
- A normal distribution is a symmetric bell curve; mean, median and mode are equal and sit at the centre.
- About 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.
- So about 34% lie between the mean and 1 SD above, about 13.5% between 1 and 2 SD above, and about 2.5% above 2 SD.
> Scores are normally distributed with mean 500 and SD 100. About what percent are between 500 and 700? Above 700? What percentile is 600?
> 700 is 2 SD above the mean: half of 95% is 47.5% between 500 and 700.
> 600 is 1 SD above: 50% + 34% = 84th percentile.
! The 68-95-99.7 figures are approximate. Pick the choice described as "about" and do not over-compute.
## Frequency distributions
- A frequency table lists each value and how many times it occurs. The number of data points is the sum of the frequencies, not the number of rows.
- Mean = sum of (value × frequency) ÷ total frequency. For the median, use running totals to find the middle position.
> Ratings: 1 (3 people), 2 (5 people), 3 (8 people), 4 (4 people). Find the mean and median.
> The median is the mean of the 10th and 11th values. Running totals: 3, 8, 16, so positions 9 to 16 are all 3. Median = 3. Mode = 3.
## Shortcuts and timing
- For "what new value keeps the mean the same" questions, the answer is the mean itself.
- For an evenly spaced list, mean = median = (first + last)/2.
- Use the calculator for a long weighted sum, but set up the sums first; most statistics QC questions need no calculation at all.
> Quantity A: the mean of 31, 32, 33, …, 49. Quantity B: the median of the same list.
> The list is evenly spaced, so the mean and median are both (31 + 49)/2 = 40. The quantities are equal.

title: Text Completion: one blank
lines: ## What you see on screen

A one-blank text completion shows a sentence or two with a gap, and below it five answer choices in a single column. You click one word or phrase. There is no partial credit and no penalty for guessing, so never leave an item blank.

These items test whether you can follow the logic of a sentence, not whether you have memorized a dictionary. Every correct answer is supported by a clue inside the sentence itself. Your job is to find that clue, decide what the blank must mean, and only then look at the choices.
## The four-step method

- Step 1: Cover the choices. Read the whole sentence first, ignoring the five words below it. If you read the choices first, each one will seem to fit for a moment, and you will talk yourself into a trap.
- Step 2: Find the clue. Ask: what word or phrase elsewhere in the sentence tells me about the blank? Underline it mentally.
- Step 3: Find the signal word. Ask: does the sentence continue in the same direction as the clue, or does it turn around?

- Step 4: Predict, then match. Put your own simple word in the blank (it can be plain, even clumsy), then choose the answer closest in meaning to your prediction. Reread the full sentence with your choice in it before moving on.
## Clue words: the evidence for the blank
The clue is the part of the sentence that describes the same thing the blank describes. Often it is a phrase that restates the blank, explains it, or gives an example of it.
> Although the senator was famous for long speeches, her reply to the reporter was strikingly ____: a single sentence, then silence.
> Clue: "a single sentence, then silence". Signal: "Although" (contrast with long speeches). Prediction: short, brief.
> An answer like "laconic" (using very few words) matches. "Verbose" is the opposite; "candid" (frank) is a real quality of a reply but is not what the clue describes.
Notice that the colon does a lot of work here. A colon, a semicolon, or a dash usually means that the next part explains or restates the earlier part, so whatever follows it is a strong clue.
## Signal words: same direction or a turn
Signal words tell you how the parts of a sentence relate. Learn them in three groups.

- Contrast (the blank is opposite to the clue): although, though, but, yet, however, despite, in spite of, while, whereas, rather than, instead of, nevertheless, far from, surprisingly, paradoxically.
- Continuation or restatement (the blank agrees with the clue): and, also, moreover, in fact, indeed, that is, in other words, not only ... but also, a colon or semicolon.
- Cause and effect (the blank follows logically from the clue): because, since, so, therefore, thus, consequently, as a result, hence, given that.
> Because the new alloy proved so ____, engineers could bend it into tight curves without any cracks forming.
> Clue: bend into tight curves without cracks. Signal: "Because" (cause). Prediction: flexible.
> "Malleable" or "pliant" fits; "brittle" is the reverse; "durable" sounds positive and technical but does not explain the bending.
> The critic, far from dismissing the debut novel, called it ____ and urged readers to seek it out.

> Signal: "far from dismissing" (a turn away from negativity). Second clue: "urged readers to seek it out". Prediction: excellent, praiseworthy. "Laudable" works; "pedestrian" (ordinary, dull) is the trap for anyone who missed the turn.

! Some sentences have no signal word at all. Then the relationship is usually restatement: the blank and the clue describe the same thing. Ask yourself what the sentence would say if you removed the blank.
## Charge and degree: two quick filters
Before you even settle on a precise prediction, decide the blank's charge: is it positive or negative? This alone often removes two or three choices.
Then think about degree: how strong must the word be? The GRE likes to offer one choice with the right charge but the wrong strength.
> The board expected mild objections to the merger; instead, shareholders were ____, flooding the meeting with angry letters and threats to sell.
> Charge: negative. Degree: strong, because "instead" contrasts with "mild" and the clue mentions a flood of angry letters.
> "Irate" or "incensed" fits. "Disappointed" has the right charge but is far too mild, so it fails the degree test.
> The results were only ____ encouraging: the drug helped a few patients slightly, while most saw no change.
> Degree words such as "only", "somewhat", "hardly" and "scarcely" shape the blank. Prediction: slightly, modestly. "Marginally" fits; "overwhelmingly" has the right direction but the wrong degree.
## Predicting when the choices are hard words

Your prediction does not need to be sophisticated. If you predict "stubborn", you can still match it to "obdurate" or "intransigent". When you do not know a choice, do not pick it simply because it looks impressive, and do not rule it out simply because it is unfamiliar. Eliminate the words you know are wrong; if one unknown word remains, it is often right.

Use word roots carefully. "Equivocal" contains "equi" (equal) and "voc" (voice), which hints at speaking with two equal voices, that is, being ambiguous. Roots can mislead, though, so treat them as a tiebreaker rather than proof.
> The witness's testimony was so ____ that each lawyer claimed it supported her own client.

> Clue: both sides could read it their way. Prediction: unclear, two-sided. "Equivocal" fits; "emphatic" is the reverse; "lengthy" is a real feature of testimony but does not explain why both sides benefit.
## Traps the GRE sets

! The opposite trap: a word that means the exact reverse of the correct answer. It catches readers who miss a contrast signal such as "although" or "far from". Always mark the signal before predicting.

! The topic trap: a word associated with the subject of the sentence (a legal word in a sentence about a trial, a scientific word in a sentence about a lab) that does not match the clue. Relevance to the topic is not evidence.
! The degree trap: the right idea at the wrong strength. "Annoyed" for "furious", "liked" for "revered".

! The second-meaning trap: the GRE often uses common words in less common senses. "Qualified" can mean limited ("qualified approval"), "check" can mean restrain, and "temper" can mean moderate. If a simple word seems to fit oddly, test its second meaning.
! The double-negative trap: phrases such as "not unwilling" or "hardly lacking in" flip twice. Translate them into plain positive language before predicting: "not unwilling" means willing.
## A full worked example
> Mitigation efforts did not eliminate the flood risk, but they did ____ it: damage in the following storm was roughly half that of the previous one.

> Step 1: Read without choices. Step 2: The clue is "damage ... roughly half". Step 3: "did not eliminate ... but they did" signals a partial success, a turn from total to partial. Step 4: Predict "reduce".
> Suppose the choices are: exacerbate, abate, eradicate, document, forecast.

> "Exacerbate" (make worse) is the opposite trap. "Eradicate" (wipe out) is the degree trap, since the sentence says the risk was not eliminated. "Document" and "forecast" are topic words linked to storms and risk, but they do not mean reduce. "Abate" (lessen) matches.
## Timing

Aim for about one minute per one-blank item, and many easy ones will take only 30 to 40 seconds. The time you save here is valuable, because reading passages need longer. If you have spent 90 seconds and are still torn between two choices, pick the one closer to your prediction, mark the item for review, and move on. You can return to marked items with the Review screen before the section ends.
## Quick checklist
- Did I read the sentence before the choices?
- What is the clue, and what is the signal (same direction, contrast, cause)?
- Is the blank positive or negative, and how strong?
- Does my choice match the prediction, and does the full sentence make sense when I reread it?

title: Text Completion: two and three blanks
lines: ## What you see on screen

A multi-blank text completion shows a passage of one to five sentences with two or three gaps, marked (i), (ii) and (iii). Under the passage there is a separate column of three choices for each blank. You click one choice in every column.

The scoring rule changes everything: you get credit only if every blank is right. Two correct blanks out of three earn exactly the same as zero. That means you must check how the blanks fit together, not just whether each choice sounds good alone.
## Why the blanks interlock

In a well-built item the blanks depend on each other. The meaning of blank (i) changes the logic of the sentence around blank (ii), and so on. Each column usually contains one choice that looks attractive in isolation but contradicts the choice another blank requires. The question tests logical structure, tone and idiom across the whole passage, so vocabulary alone is not enough.
## The method step by step
- Step 1: Read the entire passage first, ignoring all choices. Get the overall story: what is being described, and does the writer approve, disapprove or report neutrally?
- Step 2: Pick the easiest blank, not the first one. The easiest blank is the one with the strongest clue nearby. Often this is blank (ii) or (iii).
- Step 3: Predict a word for that blank and choose it from its column.
- Step 4: Plug that choice into the passage. It now acts as a new clue for the remaining blanks.
- Step 5: Predict and choose the next blank, then the last one.
- Step 6: Reread the whole passage with all your choices in place. It must read as one coherent thought. If it does not, the weak link is usually the blank you were least sure of.
## Worked example: two blanks

> Early reviewers found the composer's late quartets (i) ____, complaining that the music wandered without direction. Later scholars, however, discovered in them a (ii) ____ design: every theme returns, transformed, in the final movement.
> Blank (i) choices: incoherent, sublime, conventional. Blank (ii) choices: haphazard, meticulous, derivative.

> Start with blank (i), because its clue is right beside it: "complaining that the music wandered without direction". Prediction: aimless. "Incoherent" fits; "sublime" (awe-inspiring) has the wrong charge; "conventional" is negative-sounding but describes predictability, not wandering.

> Blank (ii): "however" signals a turn from the early complaint, and the colon tells us the design is one where every theme returns. Prediction: carefully planned. "Meticulous" fits. "Haphazard" agrees with the early reviewers, which ignores "however". "Derivative" (borrowed from others) is negative and off-topic.
Notice the interlock: anyone who chose "sublime" for blank (i) would have no logical reason for the "however" that follows.
## Worked example: three blanks, starting in the middle

> The economist's forecast was initially greeted with (i) ____; few colleagues believed that so small a change in interest rates could (ii) ____ such a large shift in spending. When the shift arrived on schedule, her critics were forced to (iii) ____ their earlier doubts.
> Blank (i): enthusiasm, skepticism, indifference. Blank (ii): precipitate, forestall, obscure. Blank (iii): reiterate, recant, conceal.

> The easiest blank is (i), whose clue is in the same sentence: "few colleagues believed". Prediction: doubt. "Skepticism" fits. "Indifference" is the trap, since doubting is not the same as not caring.
> Blank (ii): the colleagues doubted that a small change could cause a large shift. Prediction: cause. "Precipitate" (bring about suddenly) fits. "Forestall" (prevent) is the reverse.

> Blank (iii): the shift arrived as predicted, so the critics were proved wrong. Prediction: take back. "Recant" (formally withdraw a statement) fits. "Reiterate" (repeat) is the opposite; "conceal" might be tempting if you imagine embarrassed critics, but the sentence says they were "forced", which suits a public withdrawal.
## Worked example: when the easiest blank is last
> Although the museum's new wing was praised for its (i) ____, many visitors found that its very (ii) ____ made it hard to navigate; the director admitted that the design had perhaps been (iii) ____.
> Blank (i): austerity, novelty, accessibility. Blank (ii): inventiveness, plainness, convenience. Blank (iii): overly ambitious, insufficiently daring, carelessly built.

> Blank (i) has almost no clue by itself. Start with (iii): the director admits a design fault linked to being hard to navigate. "Overly ambitious" fits a design that tried too much; "insufficiently daring" is the reverse; "carelessly built" is about construction, not design.

> Now blank (ii): the quality that made it hard to navigate, and the word "very" means the praised quality and the problem are the same thing. An ambitious design is "inventive". So blank (i) must be its partner, "novelty", since the wing was praised for exactly what caused the problem.

> Check "accessibility": praising accessibility and then calling the wing hard to navigate is a contradiction, not the irony "very" signals. "Austerity" would pair with "plainness", but a plain design is not "overly ambitious". That pair fails at blank (iii), which is exactly how interlocking traps work.
## Tone and idiom

Multi-blank items often turn on tone. A passage that describes a writer "with grudging admiration" needs words that are positive but restrained, not glowing. Watch also for set phrases: one "pays tribute to" something, "falls short of" a standard, is "at odds with" a view, and something can be "anything but" simple (meaning very complicated). When a choice creates an awkward or unidiomatic phrase, be suspicious.
## Traps the GRE sets
! The lone-wolf trap: a choice that fits its own blank perfectly but clashes with the rest of the passage. The fix is the final reread with all choices in place.

! The first-blank trap: starting with blank (i) only because it comes first. If its clue is weak, you will guess, and that guess will steer the other blanks wrong. Start where the evidence is strongest.
! The partial-credit illusion: there is none. If you are certain of two blanks and unsure of the third, that third blank decides the whole item, so give it the extra 20 seconds.

! The pairing trap: the test likes to offer a matched pair of wrong answers across two columns (such as "austerity" and "plainness") that agree with each other but not with a third clue. Agreement between two blanks is necessary but not sufficient.
! The reversal trap: words such as "however", "yet" and "paradoxically" may sit between two blanks. Check whether the second blank should agree with or oppose the first.
## Timing

Budget about one minute for a two-blank item and about 1.5 minutes for a three-blank item. Across a section, this averages out to roughly one minute per verbal question when combined with faster one-blank and sentence equivalence items. If a three-blank passage still makes no sense after two minutes, choose the most consistent set you have, mark it, and return later with fresh eyes.
## Quick checklist
- Did I read the whole passage before looking at any choices?
- Which blank has the strongest clue? Start there.
- Did each new choice act as a clue for the next blank?
- Does the passage read as one logical, consistent thought with all choices in place?

title: Word problems
lines: Word problems test translation more than mathematics. Turn each sentence into an equation, label units, and check that your answer makes sense in the story. When the algebra looks long, back-solve from the answer choices.
## Translating words into algebra
- "is" means =; "of" usually means multiply; "more than" adds; "less than" subtracts in reverse order: "5 less than x" is x − 5.
- Name each unknown with a letter that reminds you what it is (t for time, c for cost).
- Write units next to numbers; mixing minutes and hours is a leading cause of wrong answers.
## Rates and speed
- Distance = rate × time. Rate = distance ÷ time.
- Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is not the average of the speeds unless equal times are spent at each speed.
- Moving toward each other, speeds add; moving the same way, subtract the slower from the faster.
> Chen drives 60 km to a lake at 40 km/h and returns the same 60 km at 60 km/h. What is his average speed?
> Time out = 60/40 = 1.5 h; time back = 60/60 = 1 h.
> Average speed = 120 km ÷ 2.5 h = 48 km/h, not (40 + 60)/2 = 50.
> Two trains 300 km apart travel toward each other at 70 km/h and 80 km/h. When do they meet?
> Closing speed = 150 km/h, so time = 300 ÷ 150 = 2 hours.
! Equal distances at two speeds always give an average below the simple mean, because more time is spent at the slower speed.
## Work problems
- Convert each worker to a rate: a job done in t hours means 1/t of the job per hour.
- Rates add when people work together: 1/a + 1/b = 1/T. A drain or a worker undoing the job subtracts.
- For two workers the together-time is ab/(a + b).
> Priya can paint a room in 6 hours and Mateo in 3 hours. How long working together?
> Rates: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 1/2 room per hour, so 2 hours.
> A pipe fills a tank in 4 hours; a leak empties a full tank in 12 hours. With both open, how long to fill it?
> Net rate = 1/4 − 1/12 = 3/12 − 1/12 = 1/6 tank per hour, so 6 hours.
! The together-time must be less than the fastest worker's time alone. An answer of 4.5 hours (the average of 6 and 3) is impossible.
## Mixtures
- Track the amount of the ingredient, not the percent: amount = concentration × volume.
- Weighted average shortcut: the final concentration sits between the two, closer to the larger quantity. The quantities are in the inverse ratio of the distances.
> How many liters of 60% acid must be added to 20 L of 30% acid to make a 40% mixture?
> Shortcut: 40 is 10 from 30 and 20 from 60, so the volumes are in ratio 20 : 10 = 2 : 1. Half of 20 L is 10 L.
## Simple and compound interest
- Simple interest: I = P × r × t, earned only on the original principal.
- Compound interest: A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ, where n is the number of compounding periods per year.
- Compound always beats simple over more than one period at the same rate.
> Olga invests $2,000 at 5% per year for 3 years. Compare simple and annual compound interest.
> What does $1,000 grow to in one year at 8% per year compounded quarterly?
! In compound questions with 3 or more periods, use the on-screen calculator; estimating 1.05³ as 1.15 is too rough when choices differ by a few dollars.
## Profit, cost and discounts
- Profit = revenue − cost. Profit percent is normally measured against cost.
- Markups are percents of cost; discounts are percents of the marked price. These are different bases.
> A shop buys a lamp for $40, marks it up 50%, then sells it at 20% off the marked price. What is the profit as a percent of cost?
> Marked price = 40 × 1.5 = $60. Sale price = 60 × 0.8 = $48.
> Profit = 48 − 40 = $8, which is 8/40 = 20% of cost.
! Up 50% and down 20% is not up 30%: the factors multiply, 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2.
## Age problems
- Use one variable for each person's age now. "In k years" adds k to everyone; "k years ago" subtracts k from everyone.
> Amara is three times as old as Kwame. In 10 years she will be twice as old as he is. How old is each now?
> Let Kwame be k, Amara 3k. In 10 years: 3k + 10 = 2(k + 10).
> 3k + 10 = 2k + 20, so k = 10. Kwame is 10 and Amara 30. Check: 40 = 2 × 20.
## Sequences
- Arithmetic (constant difference d): aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d. Sum of the first n terms = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2.
- Geometric (constant ratio r): aₙ = a₁ × rⁿ⁻¹.
- Recursive rules define each term from the one before; write out terms until you see the pattern.
> In 5, 8, 11, …, find the 40th term and the sum of the first 40 terms.
> a₁ = 3 and aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ − 1. Find a₅.
! The nth term uses n − 1 steps, not n. The 40th term is 39 differences after the first.
## Unit conversion
- Multiply by fractions equal to 1, such as (1,000 m)/(1 km), so that unwanted units cancel.
- Squared and cubed units convert with the square or cube: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10,000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.
> Convert 72 km/h to meters per second.
> A floor of 3 m² is how many cm²?
## Strategy
- Back-solve whenever the choices are numbers: plug a choice into the story and see whether every condition holds.
- Sanity-check: a time cannot be negative, a discount price must be lower, a mixture's concentration lies between its parts.
- Word problems take time. If you have read it twice and still cannot set it up, mark it, guess, and return later.
